newsitem.title: USA: Attorneys general study dividing up tobacco money.
newsitem.headline: Attorneys general study dividing up tobacco money.

text.p: America's attorneys general on Monday hailed the team that negotiated a landmark $368.5 billion settlement with the tobacco industry and began studying how to divide up the states' share of the cash.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore and other negotiators briefed their colleagues on the settlement at a closed-door meeting at a conference of the National Association of Attorneys General in Wyoming.
At the end of the meeting, the states' top law enforcement officials gave the negotiators a standing ovation.

"I think the attorneys general are very excited about this resolution. It's going to be good for the public health of this country and good for the children of this country," Moore told reporters after the meeting at a lodge in the majestic Grand Teton National Park.
Cigarette companies agreed last Friday to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years, to be divided among states, public health groups and a fund to pay damage claims of ill smokers.

The settlement, which would force the tobacco industry to curtail sharply the advertising and marketing of cigarettes and to admit the dangers of using tobacco, is being reviewed by Congress and the Clinton administration.
State attorneys general asked questions about the settlement and heard an initial proposal for dividing up the billions of dollars that will flow to the states if the agreement becomes final.

While most attorneys general commented favorably on the agreement, Minnesota Attorney General Hubert Humphrey said he did not support the settlement. "I think it can be vastly improved, and I think that it will be, and we're all going to be working to see that done," he told reporters.
He said Minnesota was continuing to pursue its lawsuit against the tobacco industry. Minnesota was one of 40 states that sued to recoup the costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.
Humphrey said he believed the dollar amount to be paid by the industry under the agreement was insufficient and he was concerned about whether the pact overly compromised individuals' rights to sue.
Indiana Attorney General Jeffrey Modisett, chairman of the group's allocation committee, said he had presented a proposal for allocating the money that would flow to the states from the agreement.

He said the attorneys general would study the proposal and raise any questions they had before their Wyoming conference ended on Thursday. The attorneys general could then refine the proposal and perhaps have another face-to-face meeting on the issue in a few weeks.
Under the proposal, all states -- not just those that filed suit -- would be entitled to share in the proceeds.

The proposed formula for deciding how much each state would get would be a blend of two figures -- the state's Medicaid spending on tobacco-related illnesses as a proportion of that figure for the nation as a whole and the state's non-Medicaid spending on tobacco-related illnesses as a proportion of national spending in that category.
The two figures would be averaged to decide how much each state receives, Modisett said.

The proposal calls for part of the "up-front" payment of about $7 billion to states to be divided according to a formula that takes account of when each state filed suit against the tobacco industry. This formula would apply only to the first payment, not to those in succeeding years.
"Those that have led the fight and taken the brunt of the responsibility here should be compensated," Modisett said.
Modisett stressed that these were only initial proposals and no decisions had been taken. He said he hoped the allocation issue would be resolved within about two weeks.
Earlier, the state negotiators hit back at critics of the settlement and said the agreement could break down if Congress made major changes.
The agreement has come under fire from some members of Congress and tobacco critics who say it is not tough enough on the cigarette companies.
